This measure is one which insures property against war risk. Who takes more war risk than the soldier, who has been denied by the minister a national system of insurance? I say he should come under this section. The committee has ignored that point altogether, but the soldier is property, and he is taking the greatest risk in this war. We must remember that the soldier is taking a greater risk than anyone else. His life, even death itself, and his property and family are at his country's service. Here we have a bill containing a number of definitions which, I submit, are purely academic, as is the whole act. I doubt if one dollar will ever be paid under this measure; in my opinion it is just like the black-outs.
The public has not been informed as to the meaning of this bill, nor have the members- all is secret, and the definitions will lead to untold litigation and relieve the insurance companies of their duty. It is not the function of parliament to deal with property and civil rights in the provinces; those are matters over which the federal parliament has no jurisdiction. Neither have we any right with respect to the law of contract or laws involving employers and employees. The committee will be wasting its time if we go any further with this measure this year, while refusing even to deal with the soldiers' insurance matter which has been on the order paper since the war began; they ignored it because the insurance companies opposed it. The standing committee which considered this measure, and accepted the definitions appearing in the bill, forgot all about the soldier who is bearing all the risk he does for the country, and gets only $1.30 a day for flying over Germany.

I agree with the leader of the opposition as to the difficulties and complications that may be involved in attempting to insure standing timber and growing crops, but I find myself also in some agreement with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. In view of the great fire hazards of modem warfare, careful consideration should be given to insuring against the cost of forest fire fighting at least, if standing timber itself is not to be insured. The greatest risk to which our natural resources are exposed in modem warfare is forest fires, especially in British Columbia. Modem warfare creates similar hazards for growing crops, which are also excluded from insurance under clause 2. This whole clause should be reconsidered and a further effort made to provide insurance against this fire risk, which is greater in this war than ever before. Fire risks in the last war and this war are not at all comparable, for reasons that are obvious.
Growing crops, especially in the vast areas of western Canada could be very seriously damaged by fire. In peace time we have hail insurance and crop insurance, and I see no reason why insurance should not be available
War Risk Insurance

for the risks which are made so much greater by our modern warfare through aeroplanes carrying incendiary bombs, by means of which vast areas of ripened grain and standing timber could be destroyed. While I appreciate the difficulty of insuring standing timber, I do think that the costs of fire fighting should be considered under this clause, as well as the insurance of growing crops.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I do not see any reason why standing timber should not be included in this bill. Some arrangement might be made with the lumbermen's association by which every lumberman of British Columbia, for example, would insure his timber at a premium commensurate with the risk. There never has been insurance for standing timber, but the hazards from fire to-day are far greater than they have ever been before, and I certainly think that those who own these tracts of timber should be entitled to have insurance to protect them. Coupled with that, the lumbermen should be forced to take proper precautions to safeguard their timber interests. Something of that kind might be worked out through the lumbermen's association.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Just a word which may not be a valuable contribution to this discussion but may be of interest to hon. members. Hon. members have said that there has been no insurance of standing timber, but I remember that in 1910 or 1911, when the firm of Price Brothers and Company made its first issue of bonds on the London market, the bond brokers insisted that insurance be placed on the standing timber, and an insurance policy was accordingly written by a group of Lloyds underwriters. Some time after that, a small fire occurred and a claim was asserted against the underwriters. The validity of the policy was contested on the ground that there had not been sufficient representations with reference to the thing insured. Action was instituted against one Mr. Heath as a test case against the various underwriters, and a commission was sent to Canada to take evidence as to the value of the property that had been destroyed by the fire. The commissioner was George H. Montgomery, K.C., of Montreal. The commission sat in Quebec, and I appeared before the commissioner to submit the evidence. I do not know that there ever was a judgment on the merits of the case. Sir William Jowitt represented Price Brothers in London, and when the case came up for trial he suggested, and I think the suggestion was accepted, that the court should first of all pronounce upon the value of the plea against the insurance 
policy. There was a decision that the insurance policy was a valid policy, and following that, I think the amount payable under the policy was adjusted. I know we were informed at that time that the underwriters of Lloyds would never again have anything to do with such a policy, and I do not think insurance has been placed on standing timber since that time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The definition of property would be sufficiently wide to cover fishing boats on both coasts were it not for the exception contained in paragraph (j) (iii). Under that definition fishing boats on the coasts cannot be insured although fishing boats on inland waters can. The main reason given in the committee for excluding coast fishing boats was that to insure them would be entering into the marine insurance business, which was pictured as a complicated business, and it was claimed that the government should not enter into such business at this time. Yet members of the committee will notice as I have said that ships on the great lakes or on other inland waters can be insured under the provisions of the bill because they are under the proviso in subparagraph (iii) of section 2 (j). I cannot speak for the eastern coast; I leave that to members representing the maritime provinces. But on the western coast our fishermen have to go out from different ports and also fish at the mouths of our rivers. Of course they are fishing in salt water, and under present war conditions they are fishing in very dangerous areas where, should there be a Japanese raid, these boats, or some of them at any rate, would be certain to suffer damage or be destroyed. The danger has been recognized by the government in that provision has been made for pensions to be payable to the fishermen, if they should be injured, or to their dependents should the fishermen lose their lives as a result of enemy action.
This fishing on the western coast is of great importance to the war effort of the united nations, because this year all the salmon and herring pack is to go to Great Britain to provide food for the British. An announcement was made in the press on March 3 of this year, quoting the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) as saying that we are going to make available to the United Kingdom all the canned salmon and herring that can be put up in 1942. So that many of these west coast fishermen are going out fishing for food for Great Britain.

War Risk Insurance
Another feature which should be considered is that to the ordinary fisherman his boat is his all. Everything he has is tied up in his boat and gear. Within the last few months, since Japan declared war, this government has arranged for the sale to white fishermen of 800 Japanese fishing boats. These Japanese boats are now being taken out by the white fishermen and will be used with the rest of the fleet in bringing in the catch this year.
It was explained in the banking and commerce committee that at the present time it is possible to get insurance on these fishing boats by obtaining it through San Francisco, but we were told that the rate to be paid as premium is either a dollar a hundred for a year, or a dollar a hundred for every three months or for thirty days. We were not given information as to which was correct, but in any event by contrast the premium under this measure was expected to be about 15 cents a hundred. So we have this position, that if no provision is made for them these fishermen will have to pay at least a dollar a hundred to get insurance through San Francisco, and the minute there is a Japanese attack the companies will probably stop issuing policies. At best therefore it is a very poor type of protection for them.
I submit to the committee that it is most unfair not to provide protection for these men. It may be that they should not be protected by this bill, though I think they should. The government should face the difficulties and provide that fishing boats can be covered under the bill. If that is not possible, I suggest that some other method must be adopted. Mr. D'Arcy Leonard, who drew this bill, and advised the banking and commerce committee throughout, made the following statement in his report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), contained in paragraph 19, referring to the question whether or not ships should be covered:
I do think however that we should canvass the possibility of making an arrangement with either the maritime shipping commission of the United States or the British war risks insurance office to make sure that cover is available at reasonable rates to Canadian hulls and on cargoes in which Canadians are interested.
It may be that this method could be adopted; that the government could make some arrangement with either of the bodies mentioned by Mr. Leonard, in order that these fishermen might get coverage at reasonable rates. Another suggestion made in the committee was that they be covered by special order in council. It was suggested that the government pass an order in council which would provide for insurance for fishing boats. I am not insisting on one method or the other
being followed, but I do submit to the minister that it is of the utmost importance that some arrangement be made to cover these fishermen, and that it be made now. We should not wait until after damage has been done to a hundred or two hundred of these boats, after they have been destroyed perhaps, to take steps to enable the fishermen to get protection. They are doing a real job not only for Canada, but also for Great Britain. They are running grave risks and are certainly entitled to protection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I think the point made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is well taken. As this war proceeds we shall find in western Canada, while the air training scheme is in operation, that some flyer is forced from time to time to land, and there is no better place in the world in which to land than a large field. In the fall of the year when there is a growing crop a fire might easily be started which would burn the whole crop. That applies too to the stook stage. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe mentioned the fact that leaflets or incendiary bombs might be dropped. We may be attacked in that way later on. The enemy may send aeroplanes and drop these things, and they might easily set fire to growing crops. The farmer should have protection. Growing crops should not be excluded. It should be possible for these men to get insurance.

I was not present at the last meeting of the committee w'hen the matter of insurance on fishing boats was discussed; unfortunately I had to attend another committee meeting. In view of the importance of the fishing fleet in procuring food for ourselves and for Great Britain, if such destruction took place and the boats were not insured, the government would have to

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I was not privileged to be a member of the committee on this bill. I would associate myself with the hon. members for Vancouver South and Vancouver East in regard to insurance on fishing vessels. In the last war we lost I think twenty-seven ships on the Atlantic coast, the direct result of German submarine activity. The fishing fleet was practically wiped out. Compensation for that loss was paid through the German reparations commission that went around the country holding hearings in 1924 or 1925. As a result of that loss and delay certain individuals and companies went into bankruptcy. The fishing fleet on the Atlantic coast suffered severely, and the industry felt that loss for a number of years.
I am a little confused as to why there should be insurance on ships on inland waters but not on those on the high seas or coastal waters. Apparently under this bill some arrangement is made whereby fishing vessels on the great lakes are to be covered. Why the distinction? There might be complication in paying partial loss as against total loss, which is what would happen in 90 per cent of the cases. I think we would be wise to make provision for that. I am thinking particularly of what took place in the last war, the great toll of fishing vessels and the resulting damage to the industry. I urge upon the minister that he see to it that something is done, if not by this measure then by some other procedure, as suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

I should like to see fishing boats included in this bill. We have along the shores of the bay of Fundy, in the counties of Charlotte, Saint John and Albert, many men who make their living-not a very lucrative living-by fishing. These men usually go out from their villages in what we used to call salmon boats, which are between twenty and thirty feet long. At present they are motor-powered and usually carry a crew of two. The boats are used for salmon and lobster fishing and for tending the sardine nets. It is quite impossible from a practical point of view for these men to take out insurance. In

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The minister in answer to a question asked by myself a few minutes ago said it was his definite understanding that these boats on the Pacific coast could be insured. I presume his information is correct, but I should like to emphasize that the expression was, insured now against war risk. We know there is insurance. The hon. member for Vancouver South placed information on the record which apparently had been submitted in committee, indicating that it is almost impossible now to obtain war risk insurance on the coast; it can be obtained only through San Francisco, which might at any moment withdraw the scheme. Also the cost is enormous.
The hon. member also brought out the fact that 800 Jap boats had been seized and sold to white people. He drew a picture of the need that there is for the protection of these boats. But that is only a portion; there is the white element too. The Jap proportion is something like 14 per cent, so that apparently there would be about 1,800 boats out in the Pacific. You can imagine how enormous the loss would be in the event of enemy action. There are hardly any boats

War Risk Insurance
that do not go out in the open sea beyond the three-mile limit, where they are exposed to all kinds of enemy attack.
Mention has been made that fishing boats on the great lakes can be insured. That puts the minister or the government, or the committee if you like, in rather an awkward position. The committee after due consideration accepted and allowed the government to insure boats on the great lakes where they are safe from enemy attack, or at any rate where attack is unlikely, but they will not do it for fishermen on the sea, where it is most needed. The hon. member for Broadview used what I thought extravagant language a little while ago when he said this measure was of no use and that nothing would be paid under it, but I am beginning to wonder whether that charge cannot in some sense be sustained. We are making a gesture about giving insurance, but when it comes to the point the real fishermen will not be insured. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare spoke of making it apply only to registered boats,, which means boats of over ten tons. That may be all right on the Atlantic, but on the Pacific coast many of our small fishing boats, although some are worth $2,500 and up, are under ten tons burden. I do not want to suggest that there is anything sinister about this thing at all; that was the last thought I had in mind, but I do find this very inconsistent. Some of those who were members of the committee have said frankly that they were not satisfied with the decision of the committee, so that it might be a matter for further consideration, to see if the words "fishing boats" could not be included. Otherwise I should like to know who gets the benefit of the act, if it is supposed to be brought in to protect the fishermen. It seems almost like the play of Hamlet with Hamlet left out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
member for Vancouver South, that the poor man out at sea fishing should be given some protection, with this war on. The definition of property does not even include those mentioned under the Farmers Creditors' Arrangement Act. It covers a dwelling up to the value of $3,000, but it does not cover a ship, except on the great lakes.
This and the preceding parliaments incorporated many insurance companies, through private bills-Canadian companies, Canadian-American companies, Anglo-Canadian and British companies-to perform the very functions covered by this act. Some of the larger companies have made fortunes out of the hundreds of millions of dollars paid in premiums on life insurance, automobile insurance, marine insurance and all the other kinds of insurance now in force. They have amassed large sums of money, and in my opinion should have been required to issue these policies and function and do this very work, though at the time the charters were issued there was some question as to whether some of the powers granted were within the jurisdiction of this parliament, since insurance is a matter of concurrent jurisdiction. But the companies will not take these risks, though they collect premiums for what I might describe as insurance against plague, pestilence, famine, battle, murder and sudden death. They even insure against certain contingencies of the weather; in the case of an exhibition or a sporting event they will insure against rain, and they do that in peace and war alike.
The trouble with this parliament is that the agents of these large insurance companies have too much influence with our committees and we forget all about soldiers and their risks. I have seen representatives of insurance companies appearing before committees to which I have belonged, submitting prepared briefs and all the rest of it. After all, this is only a small bill, limited in one respect to a total for the year of only $50,000 and in another to $3,000 for dwellings; but when you consider the work being done by these poor fishermen to whom the hon. member has referred, since the companies which should carry this insurance refuse to do so, those men should be protected by this bill. The collection or production of fish food is one of the basic industries of this country, the fisheries, in peace or war. So far as the working man is concerned, his burden is heavy enough already, with all the taxes which have been piled upon him by this government. I do not see where the minister is going to get all the money to finance this proposal, which I look upon as an improvident half-baked scheme. Within the last two years we have launched upon a large unemployment insurance scheme. Now they are trying to load up that fund, though when my leader Viscount Bennett was here they had a report that the fund was not solvent. Watch what will happen. This committee has no information before it at all. We are asked to go into something which might cost a fabulous sum of money and bankrupt the country, yet we do not know anything that took place before the committee, because their meetings were private. I do not see any reason for all the secrecy being maintained. I do not know why the questions and answers and information given to the committee could not be given to parlia-
War Risk Insurance

ment. The British parliament gets all that information. That is the trouble here. We talk about secrecy, yet the enemy know everything we do. They have their agents and envoys right here at times in this city and have full details of every statute we pass. I hope the government will get rid of this secrecy business, because it is not secrecy at all.
As I have told the minister I believe this is a scheme by which the insurance companies are endeavouring to escape from the discharge of their duties and transfer the responsibility to the federal government on this form of insurance. Fortunately in another part of this building we have a body which knows a great deal about insurance, and which I hope will give careful attention to this matter and bill.
I believe we should consider the ability of the government to carry all this and the solvency not only of this scheme but also of the unemployment insurance scheme and other similar matters. Here we have the government saying what premiums shall be paid and what property may be insured. This is a second government insurance scheme, and why should these private companies, which have collected so much money both before and since the beginning of this war, unload their responsibility on the government? The insurance companies have the profits of peace, and as sportsmen they should be prepared to take some of the losses of war. I tell you the country cannot afford this expenditure at the present time. While I approve the principle of the bill, I believe it should be laid over until next year, and in the meantime the government should attempt to force all kinds of these companies to fulfil the functions for which they received their charters and collected hundreds of millions of dollars in premiums.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
In associating myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South, I believe that those engaged in coastal fishing should be protected under this bill. In the first place the premiums to be set by the government probably will be somewhat lower than those exacted by commercial companies, and this is as much a war-time industry as any other in the country. Secondly, and more important, I should like to point out to the minister what the situation will be if losses occur among the people engaged in fishing off our coasts, if losses occur due to war risk. Their catch now I believe is subject to the price ceiling. If it is, then the cost to the government to export that catch abroad

will not be commensurate with the risk involved. It seems to me that after all it is the government's risk, and it is better that the government should give those engaged in this industry the assurance that they will be covered at a reasonable premium, perhaps not one fully commensurate with the risk but nevertheless something above the rate of 15 cents per hundred which was mentioned as the general war risk premium which might be imposed. If the coastal fishermen feel they are going to have to bear all the risk themselves, that it is not to be shouldered proportionately by the people of Canada, then if their boats are sunk or other damage is occasioned by enemy action, certainly they will not go out to bring in the fish. It is not reasonable to expect them to do so. This should be the risk of all the people of Canada. It would be better to make some provision to bring these fishermen under the bill instead of waiting until a time when the government will have to take some other action to compensate them in order to give some assurance that they will not be left to bear the whole burden themselves.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I should like the minister to explain why inland boats are included while coastal boats are not. There must be some explanation for it. As was pointed out by the last speaker, it is the duty of the whole of Canada to absorb a part of this risk. For the last two or three years on the Pacific coast, and I presume it has been the same on the Atlantic coast, these fishing boats have been used for patrol purposes in watching for enemy activities. I do not know whether they are covered in any other way, but certainly they should be protected. They have been organized in the province of British Columbia, as I suppose they have been on the Atlantic coast, into voluntary patrols. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The whole scheme of the bill is to protect property within the Dominion of Canada against damage resulting from attack, or measures taken for counter-attack. As hon. members have said, the moment one gets out of Canada and operates on the high seas, he is in an area of greater risk. It is also an area in which property may be insured at the present time through commercial channels. Marine insurance applies there. To import this class of business into inland or internal schemes of insurance would, unless we were to run grave risk with respect to the solvency of the fund, mean a considerably higher rate. It is for that reason, or a reason very much like it, that we exclude one risk to which I have referred within the dominion, namely, the risk of damage to standing trees. If we were to undertake the uncertain, perhaps very great, and possibly unascertainable liability which would be incident to placing insurance upon standing timber, we would imperil the scheme.
Ships on inland waters are covered because the risk to those ships from war is the same,
or practically the same, as the risk to buildings on the shore. In other words it is an internal risk. It is a risk which we are assuming to be equal throughout the country; that is the principle underlying the bill. It is also a risk, however, as to which a certain premium can be assigned, one which we believe would be fair for that class of risk. When we go outside, on the ocean, we are going into a most difficult and uncertain field. If we were to do that we would have to have two schemes, because in my judgment it would never do to lump ocean-going vessels, whether they were ferrying or trading vessels, with inland property. We are including property on the shores at the two ends of the dominion with property in the middle of the country. But we cannot bring too much into that class of insurance. I have repeatedly said that we do not aim to go into this business for the sake of making cheaper insurance available. If they can get insurance now, let them get it now. That is the general procedure we have followed.
A case can be made for the poor fisherman in his little boat. I do not know whether there is much likelihood of danger to that class of boat. But I do know very well that a great many of the vessels fishing on the seas are not owned by poor fishermen at all; they are owned by powerful and prosperous companies, who should be asked to take out insurance and pay for it, and who can get that insurance at the present time. If we put that class of craft into the bill we will make it much more risky for the government, and we will mix two classes of risk. Further, we will upset our principle, which is a sound one-that of not bringing in persons who can get insurance at the present time.
With regard to dealing with them separately, it is probably true that if there were any considerable or serious losses to fishermen the government would have to assume some responsibility. But we can do that by order in council at any time; we can do something appropriate under the circumstances. I do not know what we will do, because no case has been made. Nothing has been gone into in that regard, and it would have to be considered very carefully before we embarked upon a marine insurance scheme. I am prepared to give consideration to the point during the summer and see whether we should do anything in advance. We shall have to do something by order in council, in other lines, as I told the house when the bill was first introduced. We shall have to make some provision for compensation for personal injuries, and that would be done by order in council. On what basis action

War Risk Insurance

will be taken I cannot say at the present time, although a great deal of consideration has been given to the matter. There have not been any personal injuries to civilians in Canada due to enemy action.

I also see in this something of what I would term the sinister evidence of officialdom. We see this so often. When a bill is being prepared the minister says he wants certain things, but when it is being drawn up by the officials they quite often have a strong view as to the ease of carrying it out. They live by and on the boats. The minister talks now in very vague terms of doing something later on by order in council, but we should remember that to-day is the day of our salvation, to-morrow is something else. He is not going to be comforted by the vague suggestion that perhaps something will be done by order in council.
I noted particularly two sentences used by the minister. this bill is through committee he should give consideration to insuring fishermen's boats. It would not be a great risk to assume. The amount of capital involved cannot be very great, and he could protect himself by adequate premiums. Surely there must be some yardstick with which to measure. In this bill the government are giving some protection to people of limited means in other walks of life. Can they not do it for the fishermen? I beg the minister to do this. I do not agree with the hon. member, for Lethbridge that this is a rich man's bill. It is a moderate attempt to do something for all classes who may be affected by war risk. In their study of this bill hon. gentlemen have discovered that fishermen are left out, and they are making a case for the fishermen. I think they have made a good case, and I do not believe the minister has yet dealt with the concrete proposal in an adequate way. It is true that he has made the general statement that this is an experimental piece of business, and all that sort of thing, but I suggest that he become a little more realistic and give effect to what has been asked by hon. members with respect to fishermen, who need this protection.
The fishermen at the mouth of the bay of Fundy need this protection. The fishermen of the constituency of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare need it. I know the fishermen in the bay of Fundy take their large boats and go away down the bay, miles away from land. These have to be good, staunch, sturdy boats. I have watched them on the inland waters of the Pacific coast. They are a pretty substantial investment. These fishing boats are not always paid for. They represent the whole stake of the fishermen. subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR OAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Is there not a sound ground for distinction between ocean-going shipping and these deep-sea fishing boats, inasmuch as ocean-going ships can set their freight rates according to the risk involved and according to the premiums they have to pay? In other words, ocean freights are not governed by the price-ceiling regulations of our country; and though I am not yet sure of the fact, I believe the catch of the coastal fishermen is subject to the price ceiling. If insurance rates for protection against war damage rise substantially, then it will become impossible for the fishermen to operate. If they do suffer loss and are unable to replace their boats or recoup themselves financial^', they cannot be expected to go out and fish. The government want to see the greatest possible amount of fish caught by the deep-sea fishermen, because we have the canneries available and we are exporting as much of this fish as possible. Therefore the government will certainly find itself in the position of having to keep this industry going if it does suffer from enemy action. In other words, to use the vernacular, the baby is on the doorstep of the government, and the question is how they intend to provide for it. They can either bring the coastal fishermen under the bill or wait until some of them are blitzed. Then the government will have to take measures to replace the ships in order to get the raw material for our canneries and carry on our war effort.

Some hon. members said a little while ago that this measure could be held over for the summer. We are in hopes that before the

year is passed there will not be any necessity for any such insurance. It is very important that the fishermen go out now in as large numbers as possible, and with as little worry as possible about what is going to happen. On these men to a large extent depends the procuring of food for our own people and people overseas, and we should give these fishermen every encouragement. The matter should not be left dragging for months, just when we are in the real fishing season, particularly on the Pacific coast.
I urge the minister to consider what has been said, and to have an amendment brought in which would include the fishermen. Most of them do not go outside certain areas. Some of them go as far as Seattle, but they do not operate a general commercial business. They simply catch their haul of fish, bring it to the market, go out and get another haul and repeat the performance. There is not the same complication connected with the insuring of a fisherman's boat as there is with the insuring of a merchant vessel. I plead with the minister to give this matter his sympathetic and favourable consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR OAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I should like to associate myself with the leader of the opposition in advocating the extension of this insurance scheme to the fishermen. As the last speaker has pointed out, the fisherman is one of our most important producers. In many instances the loss of a boat through enemy action means the loss of everything, as regards producing not only for the war effort but for the maintenance of the fisherman's own domestic needs. I would plead with the minister to give this matter serious consideration, and have this insurance scheme applied to the fishermen.

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, May 21, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Vien in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
When I was before the committee last on May 18 I stated that I wished to deal with certain observations which the leader of the opposition had made with regard to the regulations, when he spoke on March 25. He voiced certain criticisms of the regulations, and at that time I indicated that any constructive suggestions would be cordially welcomed. A week ago Monday I indicated that I did not wish to deal, in the absence of the leader of the opposition, with the subjects that he had raised. There are one or two observations that I should like to make with regard to the criticisms which he made.
The first one with which I shall deal has to do with the reserve army. The first suggestion made by the leader of the opposition appears at the bottom of page 1638 of Hansard. He said:
That men of the trainee ages who were on the strength of a reserve unit on August 15, 1940, have not been made liable for service in Canada for the duration if they have been attending parades of their reserve units.
Then he went on to say:
I understand-the minister may correct me- that this position is still recognized; and if this excuse still obtains, the position should be changed. It is not good enough.
To a certain extent I agree with the leader of the opposition in the observations he has made. There are certain anomalies existing with regard to the particular regulation that is involved. The subject is dealt with by section 13 of the regulations. This section provides in effect that members in good standing of the reserve units who would otherwise be subject to the regulations are not called out by the divisional registrars unless or until the representative of the district officer com-

War Appropriation-War Services
manding reports that they are not performing their training in a manner satisfactory to the military authorities. The section in the regulations was enacted with the knowledge and approval of the Department of National Defence, and it has been retained in the regulations in order to enable the Department of National War Services to call out for training and service for the duration of the war men who, although discharged from the air force or the navy because of higher medical standards, are medically fit for the army. Consideration is being given to the question of how best to deal with the men who are at present in the reserve army and therefore excused, while their training is satisfactory in the reserve army, from call under the regulations. It has been suggested that these men should be pooled with other men in the callable ages and made subject to call in the ordinary way. I assure my hon. friend that the subject is under review at the present time between the Department of National Defence and the Department of National War Services.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

outset. There exist at present some anomalies and some inequities which I think are capable of adjustment.
The next subject to which the leader of the opposition referred is that of university and college students-section 17 of the regulations. This section also I think calls for revision. There are a number of subsections in section 17 which are no longer really applicable; that is, they are spent subsections, because they were enacted to meet a situation that no longer exists. Several of the subsections of section 17 relate to the state of affairs that was in existence when men were called up for only thirty days. May I say, however, with regard to section 17 generally that this section of the regulations was the result of a conference with the universities held on February 24, 1941, and there were also very full discussions with the Department of National Defence. The general basis for section 17 of the regulations is that there is a need for educated men. At present the government has found it necessary to make financial provision for certain kinds of students, namely, medical students. There is also a growing need of chemists and engineers both for army purposes and for war industries. With regard to students of that type it may become necessary to make some special provision, similar in principle to the arrangements that were made in respect of medical students.
{Mr. Thorson.]
The whole subject of students was discussed at the conference of chairmen and registrars of the various administrative divisions, held on April 23, 24, and 25, at which it was recognized that the regulations with regard to students should be revised. At that time it was suggested that the whole subject should be studied, and a further conference held with the universities and the departments having a special interest in students, which conference was held here in Ottawa on May 11. At that time it was indicated by the various departments, such as the Department of Labour, the national research council, the Department of Munitions and Supply and the departments of defence, army, navy and air, what their requirements likely would be in the matter of graduates from the universities. At this conference the universities were represented, together with the three defence departments,, the Department of Munitions and Supply, the Department of Labour, the bureau of wartime technical personnel, the national research council, and others. All had their representatives there. The director of national selective service was likewise in attendance. I think I may assure the committee that the regulations will be revised in the light of the existing situation.

When the Military Service Act of 1917 was brought down, the plan, the modus operandi, the method by which the draft was'to take place, was submitted to parliament, where it underwent thorough revision by the representatives of the people. Does the minister not think that is the democratic way in which this should be done? I suggest to him that the methods by which men shall be drafted into the army under a compulsory system, such as is now' in force in this country to a limited degree, could and should be brought into the House of Commons, where the representatives of the people could have something to say about these regulations; how they shall be prepared; how they shall be put into effect, and be given a chance to criticize their operation.
What happens now? A departmental committee, as the minister has indicated, drafts a regulation, wdiich is adopted by order in council and becomes an accomplished fact before we know anything about it. Take this vexed question of farmers' sons. Under the regulations as adopted by order in council, until a comparatively recent date it was impossible to get anything in the way of exemption for a farmer's son.

I used the word "exemption" advisedly. It was possible to get a postponement for a limited period of time, and perhaps several postponements, but anything in the nature of a complete exemption was impossible. I illustrate that by the case of a young man who was an only son, whose father had died, who was milking thirty cow's, and who was called up in the draft. That was in the days of the thirty-day training period. He and his mother came to see me. I explained that he could get a postponement and probably a certain number of postponements, but that he could not get indefinite postponement. I advised him, if he could possibly hire anyone to do the work, to take his thirty-day training in the winter season rather than depend on getting further postponements later on. He took his training. I do not know whether he has been called up again, but that is the case of a boy who was producing food of high quality and value. If he had been called up under the present draft system, his mother would have had to simply fold up; she could not
possibly carry on. That was one of the iniquities of a system adopted secretly by order in council, without the representatives of the people having a single word to say about it.
That system is wrong. Any regulations having to do with the drafting of men ought to be brought by the administration to parliament. Let parliament take the responsibility; let parliament pass upon such regulations. The whole theory of doing these things by order in council is wrong. I put myself in the judgment of members of this house if I am not right in that statement, and: whether in their secret hearts they will not support me in that position. I am sure I am right about this. I am as anxious to see a complete, allout war effort as any man in this house, and I have been consistent in that regard right along. But I realize that we cannot take every man for the army. Every man should go to his place, and his place is conditioned by circumstances. But to say that a group of officers or officials here in Ottawa can sit round a table and frame a system of regulations, and that we cannot do that here in this house-well, it is just common nonsense; that is all. More than that, there is a great principle at stake here. The drafting of men for military service is a very important operation, which ought not to be left in the hands of a group of officials who are not responsible to the people. That is a sound principle I am laying down. It must and should be-done in a democratic country like Canada under a system whereby these regulations before they become law shall be drafted as the basis of discussion, and brought before parliament.
What happened in 1917? They were brought before parliament in that year; and if hon. members will look at Hansard for those days they will see that those regulations were-debated and revised and improved, and that many valuable suggestions came from the membership of the House of Commons before the regulations were finally put into operation. That is the course I ask this government to* pursue, not only in the revision of regulations, as they stand to-day, but in any future-regulations which may be enacted as the result of legislation at present pending before this house.
I put it up to the House of Commons tonight, that this drafting of regulations for the conscription of man-power by the government of this country-and we have conscription by this government; not quite full yet, but that will come-should be done by a democratic body, like the House of Commons, and should not be done in the secrecy either

of a caucus or of cabinet council. I defy anybody successfully to combat that theory. We will very soon see that something like justice is done to all classes in the community, and that there will be equality in service, so far as manpower is concerned. I do not think we can get the same measure of equality if this sort of thing is done secretly by order in council; and I object to such a method.

I do not think he can accuse me of doing so, as far as this resolution is concerned, because on only two occasions, I think, have I said anything other than to ask a few questions. But to-night I am going to bring to his attention what I think is an important matter, because it deals with the provision of labour to take off the coming harvest. Some hon. members may think it is a little early to talk of this, but I do so because it is quite evident that it takes the minister's department and certain departments of the government quite a long time to get organized to do anything efficiently and in proper season. May I say also that this matter is brought to my attention through having received recently a number of letters similar to that mentioned by

the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar a while ago. I have a number in my desk, I am not going to take time to read them, but one or two I shall refer to briefly.
Farmers have completed their seeding operations in spite of difficulties as far as labour is concerned. Great credit is due them that they have done as well as they have in getting a crop in. The seeding is pretty well all done in western Canada, the season has been favourable so far, and the outlook is for an average crop. But there is going to be a critical situation in harvest time. An order in council that has been discussed at considerable length on different occasions in the last three or four weeks was tabled, I think, on March 25. It is P C. 2251, and one clause of it was for the purpose of freezing employment in agriculture. Prior to that date the records show that enlistments in western Canada-and I am going to deal more particularly with the three prairie provinces-were very great; that is, very favourable compared with the rest of Canada, especially among the farmers. Also industry in eastern Canada had taken quite a toll of farm labour and farmers' sons. Many of them came east and got employment in industry, where they receive good wages. There has been considerable discussion of that order in council, and suggestions have been made that possibly another order should be passed, to all intents and purposes making that order retroactive at least eight months. However, that is a matter for the government to decide. I make the suggestion now that something of that kind might be done.
However, prior to that order being passed, many men had come from western Canada and secured positions in industry. Girls and women have also enlisted and come from the west, particularly the prairie provinces, in great numbers. Here in Ottawa many girls from the west are in offices. Their brothers have enlisted; they have a patriotic spirit; they come here and get a position or enlist. It may be of interest to hon. members to learn that women and girls can play a very important part in harvesting operations. Harvesting this year will be somewhat different from that in other years. The farmers have met the suggestions and regulations put out by the Department of Agriculture, they have complied with what the Minister of Agriculture asked them to do in increasing their seeding of coarse grains and flax. These crops cannot be harvested like wheat; they require more labour. Wheat now is generally "combined", and one man can do a great deal, taking the place of a dozen or more in harvesting. But that cannot be done with respect to coarse grains, they have to be cut with the binder,
stooked and so on. In the last few years girls and women have played a very important part in harvesting operations, but now many of them have enlisted or left the farms for other positions.
The question of university students was mentioned. I have here a note from one of the western papers which states that since January last a great many students have been leaving school to get employment before they should be barred from restricted occupations. Quite a number of farmers' sons of seventeen years of age and under have left school on that account and now are not available to help in the harvest. I know that representations have already been made to the Minister of Agriculture asking him to cooperate with the minister now before the committee to see that regulations are formulated to deal with this matter. There should have been regulations similar to order in council P.C. 2251 freezing farm employment a year ago. We should now have some understanding and a statement from the minister, before this resolution passes, as to what he proposes to do. His department is, I believe, conducting a national registration of unemployed between the ages of sixteen and seventy-

In addition, there have been many enlistments of farmers and farmers' sons; their showing has been very creditable. As a result there is a dearth of labour available to take off the harvest. The Minister of National Defence also said definitely that harvest leave would not be granted to those in the active service forces in Canada. We have no objection at all to that, but it is evident that there will be no leave granted for harvest leave. So I want the minister, now that he is registering the unemployed between sixteen and seventy, to use those figures to mobilize the man-power and woman-power of Canada so that sufficient may be available to the west to assist in taking off the harvest.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister now. He may smile, but his record for action does not warrant any smiling. This is an important matter, and we are going to have an acute situation in the west with respect to labour. It is a serious matter now, and I bring it to the attention of the minister only because I want action. According to the letters I have received, the farmers are very much concerned about how they are going to get along. I come from a real farming country, where there is a real shortage of labour, in particular for dairy farms. I cannot quite appreciate any shortage on the prairies, because I understood we in this house were arranging to have all the prairie farms summer-fallowed, or something like that. Where I come from this shortage is very serious; but before I go on with that I want to take up my controversial subject.
I am very much interested in learning what the minister intends to do with regard to conscientious objectors in British Columbia. Any explanation the minister has given me so far in answer to my questions along this line certainly has not been satisfactory either to me [DOT]or to my constituents or, I think, to the people of British Columbia as a whole. In my province the people who presumably were to be called up by the minister's department have all gone into the shipyards or other highly paid employment-and for the benefit of any hon. member who might question me I do not say too highly paid, nevertheless highly paid positions. These men obtain, in many cases, the benefits of a high rate of wages; 98 cents an hour, to be accurate. They happen to be exempt by law from military service; they do not have to carry out the duty of any ordinary citizen, that of defending his own country. They are exempted by law from having to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member should be more careful in his statements. They are postponed in respect of their military training if they show that they are Mennonites or Doukhobors within the meaning of section 18 of the regulations, or conscientious objectors within the meaning of section 19. That arises only when they have been called up under the regulations. Then, if their claim is recognized, as a Mennonite or Doukhobor or conscientious objector, they are held for alternative service in work camps; and when they are directed to that alternative service, which may now be for the duration of the war, they receive 50 cents a day.

With all due deference to the minister I must say that he is not correct in his assumption. I presume he has been ill advised by his department. That is not correct in British Columbia, whatever may be the situation in the rest of Canada.
This is the original call that came-I deliberately avoided using names; but since the minister has put them on record, I will say they were conscientious objectors. I will now tell the minister how they were exempted from service-and this is a very serious matter. The minister may think it is not serious, but certainly it is serious to the mothers of the boys in England to-day, or of those who may not come back. It is a very serious matter to them.
Under our so-called mobilization act I think the age was twenty-one to twenty-four; is that not correct? They were called up from twenty-one to twenty-four years; but the minister apparently never heard of twenty-five years of age.

Pardon me; you are speaking of the present time. I will leave it to the committee as to whether the minister was correct or not. Sometimes it pays to wait until all the facts are put before one, and then attempt to answer them; not to jump in ahead of time. The original measure called for men from twenty-one to twenty-four. A boy twenty-four years and two days old could go into a shipyard at 98 cents an hour. He did not have to apply for exemption; he did not go to an army camp at 50 cents a day-and I defy the minister to contradict that. Mark that; I do not say he is incorrect-certainly not. I do not say that, but I will put it that he is ill advised. However, it is not an assumption that should be put as stated by the minister; the age was not originally thirty years. They were not called up; they were not called into these army camps-I am referring to the boys who happened to be twenty-four years and one day old.
They went into the shipyards. Then what happened? Because this act did not function as some of us in the rump suggested a year ago it should act-that is, it did not bring in national selective service at the proper time- these men went into the shipyards and other highly paid war industries, with the result that they are now classed as essential war workers, skilled workmen, carpenters and shipbuilders. Some of them never saw a ship in their lives, unless it was in a movie. But now they are classed as skilled workmen because they are working in those shipyards. I could give the minister the names of plenty of them in war industry who have not had to get exemption. I do not think it is a proper practice, and the minister has yet to show me any excuse for it.

War Appropriation-War Services
I would be interested in hearing the minister's-I will not call it an excuse; possibly I should say I would be interested in hearing him try to explain to me that they are exempted only through postponement. Then we go on to those men thirty years and one day old. By an act of parliament these conscientious objectors are given exemptions from defending their country. I am not blaming the present minister, the present government or possibly the past government. I believe it was pointed out that the provision was made in 1873. But I must urge the seriousness of the situation, a seriousness which unfortunately the minister has not yet grasped. I should like to make myself particularly clear to the hon. member for Vancouver East. Let hon. members bear in mind that I am not quarrelling with the unions, either. I have a great respect for the unions, because I believe in collective bargaining. The labouring man would have a terrible time to-day if he did not have his union to protect his interests.
These conscientious objectors are allowed to avoid military service to defend their country. However, they go into a shipyard and automatically they must join unions. Any man who applies for any position must join one of the unions. I have no quarrel with the unions, or with the principle of collective bargaining which I strongly endorse; but I do say that once these men are in the shipyard unions, they can tie up the most essential war industry we have in Canada or in the British empire, namely that of shipbuilding. Surely, if a man has the right to strike and to tie up a war industry, he should not have the right to exemption from service to his country. I should be interested to hear the minister's explanation of that.
I have a question in mind which I could direct to the hon. member for Parkdale. He might think I do not know anything about this matter. Erankly I do not know much about it, but I have noticed that a number of members talk about many things concerning which their knowledge is limited. I should like to know how young doctors from twenty-one to thirty years of age are treated, so far as their calls for military service are concerned. I have information from certain medical men in British Columbia that there is a need, estimated by the Department of National Defence, for some 600 medical men in the current year. I am also told that medical authorities in that department say that at the present time there is an urgent need for 200. I presume those figures are correct.
I should like it to be understood that I am not criticizing the medical profession or the

minister's department. I am asking for information. The information which comes to me has given me certain figures, and I am also advised that in British Columbia there is an advisory council of medical men and, I believe, a central advisory council for Canada, whose duty it is to advise so that doctors will not enlist and leave any part of Canada without proper medical service. That is my information.
I cannot see why young doctors under thirty years of age should be in a position to avoid the call, stay at home and take the practices of many doctors, particularly in the city of Vancouver, who have wonderful practices built up by themselves, but who have answered the call and gone away. I see no reason why these young men under thirty years of age should be allowed to stay at home and walk into those practices, while the original practitioners are serving overseas. I am speaking from information given to me by practical medical men of my province.

speechtext: I shall try to deal briefly with the two questions put by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. The first one which relates to doctors I think can be answered in just a sentence or two. speechtext: I understand that the minister's department issues a requisition for a certain number of men in a certain district. Under what plan does the registrar call up the number required? Are they called alphabetically or how?

Each division is comprised of a certain number of electoral districts, and the registrar is asked to distribute the quota he must fill as equitably as possible over his whole division and call men according to juniority.
To come back to conscientious objectors, the question as to whether a man is or is not a conscientious objector does not arise for anybody to determine in respect of persons who are not in the callable age group. My hon. friend is quite right when he says that persons of, say thirty-one years of age might be employed in a shipyard. No one will have determined whether such a man is a conscientious objector because he has not applied for postponement of his military training. There is no automatic postponement in respect of any class of persons. In each case there is an individual decision made by the board in respect of an application for postponement of military training on the grounds of conscientious objection.
In our attitude toward conscientious objection we are taking exactly the same attitude as that taken by every civilized country in the world, and we intend to continue to take that civilized attitude. I doubt if there is a single man in this house who can understand in himself the point of view of a conscientious objector; nevertheless we think we are all determined that we should adopt an attitude toward conscientious objection similar to that adopted by other civilized countries. I have yet to learn of an employer in this country

asking any person as a condition precedent to his employment what his attitude is toward the bearing of arms. The question of conscientious objection does not arise.
These men are as good workers as any other men. Hundreds of so-called Mennonites have enlisted for active service anywhere in the world. A great number have indicated their desire to undertake the most dangerous service possible, notwithstanding the fact that they have conscientious objection to the bearing of arms or the taking of human life. The situation which my hon. friend brings to my attention is one that we cannot criticize. These men are good workmen, and they are not subject to call for the time being any more than anyone else in the same age group. But when we move the age group up-

It seems to me that one of the functions of this department is to take into consideration the total man-power and other resources of the dominion and then to work out plans that will result in the most effective war effort. I can understand that the Minister of National Defence quite rightly thinks that the most important department in the war effort is national defence, and the same thing applies to the minister for air and the minister for naval services. The Minister of Munitions and Supply has also a tremendous programme, and the Minister of Agriculture is naturally concerned about producing food for Canadians and for the people of Great Britain. It therefore seems to me that the Department of National War Services should be the one department able to view the entire field and to work out the most effective plans. I have been puzzled as to why national plans have not been worked out more effectively. Reference has been made to the orders in council and to the minister's memorandum in connection with the manpower policy as it applies to agriculture. But still I do not think we have a department here that is planning the most effective things that can be done. I cannot understand why the board in Regina should be the final authority to decide what the agricultural policy of Canada shall be or what the agricultural policy for Saskatchewan shall be.
Yesterday I received an airmail letter in connection with a young man who had just turned twenty-one last December. He and his father are on a 320-acre farm. This lad received his medical call on April 21. He applied for postponement and on May 17 received a letter stating that his postponement was refused. On May 20 he received his ticket and a notice to be in Prince Albert on May 21, less than twenty-four hours after he had received his ticket. His family had read in the Winnipeg Free Press that we are not calling any more farm boys who are engaged in agriculture. I am not familiar with that farm or with the family, but according to the letter I have received, the father cannot, without help, carry on operations on that farm with ten horses and two outfits. The young man has been called, and now that he is in the army he goes into another category. The army authorities, I suppose, are not kindly disposed toward granting him any postponement for any extended period. So that in spite of the announced policy of this government regarding the necessity of keeping men on the farm to carry on our agriculture production programme, it would appear to me that the board in Saskatchewan can, as matters now stand, ignore this statement of policy of the government. The board does not have to prove to any particular applicant that the applicant, to use the exact words of the memorandum, "is not an essential worker in agriculture." If the
board in Regina with the evidence before them say that this man is not essential in agriculture, that closes the subject and the man is called. If I am to judge by the remarks which the chairman of the board made to me last January, his opinion is that every able-bodied man should be in the army.
I think some responsible department of the government should decide the maximum number we require in the army. I am not suggesting that we have that maximum number now; but sooner or later some responsible department will have to make that decision, and when we do reach the maximum number required for the army we should retain on the farms a sufficient number of men to carry on the farming industry to supply the needs of the army and of civilian life in this country and our needs overseas. I wish the minister would announce a policy which could be carried out all across Canada with respect to retaining on the farm however many men are needed there. Now that we have disposed of this one man case that has taken up so much time, I must say that I was pleased indeed to hear the minister say a few days ago that this was a mobilization act, not a demobilization act. One sitting in this house and listening to a great many of the remarks made would almost think we were more interested in keeping men out of the army than in getting them into it. We have shown a great deal of sympathy for conscientious objectors. I am proud to say that in my own province we have very few of these people. Out of some six thousand men whom I have had at my military camp, we have had less than half a dozen conscientious objectors. It seems to me that a great deal of sympathy has been expressed in this house for people of this class, one might almost say maudlin sympathy, indeed more than has been expressed for the men who are really trying to do their duty and carry on the work that is necessary.
We have little complaint in New Brunswick, where we have an efficient registrar and an efficient board, of which Chief Justice Baxter is chairman. There is a question I should like to ask, however, in connection with farm labour, following what has been said by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and some other hon. gentlemen. My question is with regard to the distribution of farm labour. There are certain sections of my province- and I am satisfied that the same thing is true all over Canada-where the farms have been almost depleted of men. I believe that is particularly so in the Kennebecasis valley, in my own constituency, and up the St. John river in the other part of the province. Those sections have been drained of practically all the young men who were on the farms, and I may add that these are the best farming sections in the province. In my constituency we have large dairy farms with practically no help. Up the St. John river there are the large potato farms, also with practically no help. But then we have other sections where there are smaller farms, perhaps 100 or 120 acres, and it is from these sections that most of the applications for postponement are coming. On some of these farms there are five or six men, yet they are asking for exemption and getting it. On the one hand, in certain sections we have small farms with numbers of men on them and, on the other hand, large farms, with practically no men.
My question to the minister is this. How is he going to distribute this labour? The same thing applies to labour in the west. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said that in certain sections the farms have been practically depleted of men. Is labour to be taken
from one section of Canada and placed in another? Is it to be distributed evenly over a province? After all, there is no use in saying that we are going to hold so many men on the farms if on one farm there is no labour at all and on another, a smaller farm, there are more men than are really required. As I understand it, these men must be engaged in farm labour. I believe this is a problem which the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of National War Services will have to take into consideration. Something will have to be done in order to have a proper distribution of the farm labour which has been frozen on the land.

That is not going to be the easiest problem to deal with; indeed it is an exceedingly difficult one. It is part of the problem of utilizing man-power to the fullest possible extent, where questions of the mobility or immobility of man-power are involved. It is undoubtedly true that in some areas of Canada the supply of agricultural labour has been so much depleted that the situation is very serious, while in other parts of Canada the situation is not quite so bad. The departments vitally concerned are the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Labour and my own department to the extent that the calling up of men may make inroads upon the supply of agricultural labour. We tried by the adoption of the agricultural policy that underlies order in council P.C. 2252 to prevent any further drain upon agricultural labour, in the hope that if we could prevent the agricultural situation across Canada from getting any worse we could get by-not any more than that-with our agricultural commitments that are part of our war effort. For that reason we decided that we would stabilize employment in agriculture, as far as possible, of persons who are wholly or mainly employed in agriculture and, subject to certain exemptions, prevent them from leaving agriculture. In other words, using language that perhaps is not exact, we were freezing them in agriculture. I will admit that this does not fully meet the

situation in the areas which have been too greatly depleted, but that is a situation which will demand our very best attention.

There is a plethora of men in that community, while in the county of Kings you cannot hire a man to milk a cow to save your soul. This situation must be dealt with.

speechtext:
I
should like to speak concerning a different subject entirely. What is the minister going to do in regard to the Canadian women's voluntary services? This organization was formed in June, 1941, and was registered under the War Charities Act in September of that year. Since that time these women have done a wonderful work, and are continuing to do it to-day. Now, however, the government seems to disregard them entirely, and wants to take over what the women have been doing. Instead of its being on a voluntary basis, the government has now engaged a Mrs. West as director at a salary of $4,000 a year, and has appointed an assistant at a yearly salary of
83,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Plus expenses. These C.W.V.S. women have carried on their work, especially across Ontario, at no expense whatsoever to the government. They have given their time, service and everything else.
In his letter of April 27, 1942, to the president of the Canadian women's voluntary services at Toronto the minister says:
It was finally decided to establish a division of the Department of National War Services to be known as the division of women's voluntary services. This division was established by order in council P.C. 8488, dated October 31, 1941.
That was only a month after the Canadian women's voluntary services had been registered under the act. However, the government did not tell the women about it at that time, and they have been carrying on ever since. They are now wondering what is going to-happen to them. Another part of the minister's letter states:
I have therefore approved of the organization and development of the division of women's voluntary services as outlined in the attached memorandum. A study of this memorandum will indicate that the approach of your organization to coordination of women's voluntary effort is the exact opposite to that of our division. In the past ten days Mrs. West and Miss Held have been visiting many of the Ontario communities and find there is a great deal of confusion because of the similarity in name of the two organizations.

War Appropriation-TV'ar Services
I am therefore waiting to advise you that much as I regret to take this action, it will be necessary for my department to terminate the registration of your organization under the War Charities Act under its present name

"Canadian women's voluntary services".
We would, however, be pleased to consult with you as to methods of cooperation from your organization, under some other name, in furthering the objects of the women's voluntary services division of the Department of National War Services.
This letter is signed by J. T. Tliorson. The government stepped in, after these women had organized and done all the spade work. The government step in and say, "Your name is out; we will take it over."
The next letter is from the president of the Ontario association. I shall not read that letter, but shall proceed to the next one sent by the minister. This letter is dated May 4, 1942, and states:
First, I pointed out that the similarity in name between the "division of women's voluntary services" in the Department of National War Services and that under which you have been operating-"Canadian women's voluntary services, (Ontario division)"-is leading to confusion.
There would not have been any confusion if the government had just checked back over their files and found out that the women had registered a month before.

All voluntary services. Mrs. Roberts, chairman of Canadian women's voluntary services for Ontario, wrote a letter to the Minister of National War Services, and this is part of what she said:
Your department says "perhaps it would be a good idea to have some courses for emergencies set up and when the emergencies arise give the courses of training." This programme of preparedness which we have adopted is what your department regards as "overstimulation of volunteer effort."

War Appropriation-War Services
Miss Margaret Hyndman, K.C., and Mrs. Murdoch MacKenzie came to Ottawa and saw Mrs. West and Miss Held, and this is part of their report:
(1)	That the government's plan is to have women's war work done in communities by social agencies;
(2)	That no war work should be undertaken in a community until these social agencies who have their "ear to the ground" as to the needs, give the word "go";
(3)	That women should not be trained for emergencies now, nor their free time utilized for war work except such "unspectacular" (as she called them) -
That would be Mrs. West.
-and relatively unimportant jobs as salvage and price control enforcement. Nor should they be encouraged to organize their lives to have free time which can be so utilized.
